q: In a lab, trained observers listen to a metronome and carefully report each click as a set of basic sensations, images and feelings. The researcher wants to map the building blocks of conscious experience. Which school of thought does this best represent?
opts: Functionalism, as developed by William James
Structuralism, as developed by Titchener
Gestalt psychology, as developed by Wertheimer
Behaviourism, as developed by John B. Watson
why: Breaking experience into sensations, images and affections is Titchener's structuralism. Functionalism is tempting because it is also an early school, but it asks what the mind does to help us adapt, not what elements it is made of.

q: Puan Siti, a counsellor, tells her client Danial that he is free to choose a new path after failing his first semester, and that their work is about helping him become his full, actual self. Which perspective is she using?
opts: Psychodynamic perspective
Cognitive perspective
Behavioural perspective
Humanistic perspective
why: Free will and self-actualisation are the core ideas of the humanistic 'third force' (Maslow, Rogers). Psychodynamic is tempting because it also deals with the self, but it focuses on unconscious motivations and early experience rather than free choice.

q: A researcher argues that people in every culture fear snakes and heights because ancestors who avoided them were more likely to survive and reproduce. Which perspective is she taking?
opts: Biopsychological perspective
Evolutionary perspective
Sociocultural perspective
Behavioural perspective
why: Explaining a universal trait by its adaptive or survival value is the evolutionary perspective. Biopsychological is tempting because it is also biological, but it explains behaviour through current bodily events such as hormones or nervous-system activity, not survival history.

q: Mei Ling is a participant in a HELP study. Halfway through a stressful timed task she says she wants to stop, even though she signed the consent form. Under common ethical guidelines, what should happen?
opts: She must finish because her consent form is binding
She may stop only after the researcher debriefs her fully
She may withdraw immediately without having to finish
She may stop only if the review board approves first
why: Participants may withdraw at any time, regardless of having consented earlier. Debriefing is also a guideline, but it is not a condition she must meet before she is allowed to leave.

q: A HELP lecturer plans a study in which participants are briefly misled about its true purpose. Before any data are collected, what is most likely to happen?
opts: The study is automatically rejected because deception is banned
An ethics review board judges whether the deception is justified
Participants are told the hypothesis so consent is not needed
The study goes ahead and is reviewed only after it is published
why: Institutional review boards (e.g. the HELP Ethics Review Board) review each proposed study, and deception is allowed only if it is justified and followed by debriefing. Deception is not automatically banned, so the rejection option is wrong.

q: Aina has severe depression and her doctor thinks medication may help. Which professional can prescribe it, and why?
opts: A psychiatrist, because a psychiatrist is a medical doctor
A psychologist, because a Ph.D. licence allows prescribing
A psychiatric social worker, because they hold an L.C.S.W.
A psychologist, because they specialise in clinical disorders
why: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor and can prescribe medication. A psychologist is tempting because many treat disorders, but a psychologist holds a Ph.D., Psy.D. or Ed.D. and typically doesn't prescribe.

q: A therapist explores how Encik Lim's sense of self formed in childhood and what motivates his choices, with little attention to sexual urges. Why is this psychodynamic rather than classic psychoanalysis?
opts: It rejects the unconscious and studies only behaviour
It focuses on the self and motives, not sexual motivations
It was developed by Freud himself in his early clinic
It explains behaviour through hormones and genes
why: The psychodynamic perspective is the modern version of psychoanalysis and focuses on the developing self and motives rather than sexual motivations. Rejecting the unconscious and studying only behaviour describes behaviourism, not psychodynamics.

q: Danial studies how memory helps first-year students adapt to university life. Why does this fit functionalism rather than structuralism?
opts: It asks what the mind does to help people adapt
It breaks memory into sensations, images and affections
It holds that the whole is greater than its parts
It studies only behaviour that can be directly measured
why: Functionalism (William James) asks how the mind helps people adapt, live, work and play. Breaking experience into sensations, images and affections is structuralism, the very school this example contrasts with.

q: A baby who showed no fear of a white rat began to cry at the sight of it after the rat was repeatedly paired with a loud noise. Which claim does this case most directly support?
opts: Freud's claim that phobias come from repressed urges
The claim that fears are universal survival traits
Watson's claim that phobias are learned
Wundt's claim that consciousness has basic elements
why: Little Albert was Watson's demonstration that a fear (phobia) can be conditioned, i.e. learned. Freud's explanation is tempting because it also concerns phobias, but the fear here was produced by pairing, not by repressed urges.

q: People recognise the song 'Negaraku' instantly even when every note is shifted into a different key, so no single note is the same as before. Which school does this finding best support?
opts: Structuralism
Functionalism
Gestalt psychology
Behaviourism
why: Recognising the tune even though every element changed shows the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, the Gestalt claim. It weakens structuralism, which assumes experience can be understood by breaking it into its basic elements.

q: Three of these researchers follow common ethical guidelines. Which one does NOT?
opts: Explains the study to participants after using deception
Stores participants' answers under codes, not names
Explains risks clearly before participants sign consent
Tells a participant she can't leave because she was paid
why: Participants may withdraw at any time, so refusing to let someone leave breaks the guidelines. Debriefing after deception is not a violation; it is the required follow-up when deception is justified.

q: Three of these studies take a sociocultural perspective. Which one does NOT?
opts: Measuring cortisol levels in students before SPM exams
Comparing how Malaysian and Australian students question lecturers
Studying how roles in a futsal group shape members' behaviour
Comparing cultural norms about eye contact with elders
why: Measuring a hormone such as cortisol explains behaviour through biological events in the body, which is the biopsychological perspective. The futsal group study may look less 'cultural', but social roles and groups are part of social psychology within the sociocultural perspective.

q: Aina touches a hot pot. A neuron in the centre of her spinal cord receives the pain signal and passes a command to the neurons that move her arm away. What type of neuron is this?
opts: Interneuron
Sensory (afferent) neuron
Motor (efferent) neuron
Glial cell
why: Interneurons sit in the centre of the spinal cord, receiving input from sensory neurons and sending commands through motor neurons. A sensory neuron is tempting, but it only carries information from the senses to the CNS; it doesn't pass commands on to motor neurons.

q: While Danial solves a hard calculus problem, certain cells widen nearby blood vessels so the busy brain area receives more nutrients. Which cells are doing this?
opts: Astrocytes
Microglia
Oligodendrocytes
Radial glia
why: Astrocytes control blood flow and dilate blood vessels during heightened activity. Microglia are tempting because they are also glial cells that remove waste, but they act like an immune system and don't regulate blood flow.

q: A neuron at rest receives a stimulus that depolarises it to just below its threshold of excitement. What will most likely happen?
opts: A small action potential is fired
No action potential is fired
A full action potential fires slowly
The neuron enters hyperpolarisation
why: Below threshold there is no action potential, and by the all-or-none law there is no partial version. A small action potential is tempting, but action potentials fire at full strength or not at all.

q: Right after a neuron fires, a researcher applies a very strong stimulus during its absolute refractory period. What will happen?
opts: It will fire because the stimulus is strong
It will fire a weaker action potential
It will fire faster than usual
It won't fire, however strong the stimulus
why: During the absolute refractory period a neuron cannot fire again regardless of stimulation. 'It fires because the stimulus is strong' describes the relative refractory period, when a stronger-than-usual stimulus is needed.

q: A light touch and a hard pinch both trigger action potentials of the same size in Mei Ling's sensory neurons, yet the pinch feels stronger. How is the difference coded?
opts: Larger action potentials for the pinch
Faster action potentials for the pinch
Longer-lasting depolarisation per spike
More frequent firing and more neurons firing
why: Within a neuron, action potentials have equal intensity and speed, so strength is coded by firing frequency and the number of neurons firing. 'Larger action potentials' is tempting, but the all-or-none law rules it out.

q: Encik Lim's damaged nerve in his forearm slowly recovers, but a patient with myelin damage in the spinal cord does not. What best explains the difference?
opts: CNS oligodendrocytes can repair; PNS Schwann cells may not
Forearm nerves have no myelin, so nothing needs repair
PNS Schwann cells can repair; CNS oligodendrocytes may not
Microglia rebuild myelin in the PNS but not in the CNS
why: Schwann cells (PNS) can reconnect and repair themselves, while oligodendrocytes (CNS) are more likely to be permanently damaged. The reversed option is tempting because both cell types build myelin, but it swaps their locations.

q: Researchers find that a drug which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels prevents a neuron from producing any action potential. What does this support?
opts: Depolarisation depends on potassium rushing in
Resting potential depends on sodium flowing in
Depolarisation depends on sodium rushing in
Action potentials depend on chloride flowing out
why: In an action potential, sodium channels open and sodium rushes in, making the inside positive (depolarisation). Potassium is tempting, but potassium rushing out is what causes repolarisation and hyperpolarisation, not depolarisation.

q: Recordings show that along a myelinated axon, the action potential is regenerated only at small unmyelinated gaps and travels faster than along a bare axon. Which concept does this support?
opts: Spreading from the axon hillock along bare membrane
The all-or-none law of neural firing
Saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
The relative refractory period
why: Regeneration only at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), with a jump from node to node that boosts speed, is saltatory conduction. The axon hillock is tempting because action potentials begin there, but that doesn't explain jumping between gaps.

q: A patient's nerve messages have become slow and unreliable. Tests show the fatty coating that insulates his axons is breaking down. Which part of the neuron is affected?
opts: Dendrites
Myelin sheath
Soma and nucleus
Axon terminals
why: The myelin sheath is the fatty coating that insulates the axon and speeds up impulses, so its loss slows conduction. Axon terminals are tempting, but they communicate with other cells; they are not the insulating coat.

q: A toxin stops potassium channels from opening after an action potential peaks. What is the most likely result?
opts: The neuron can't depolarise in the first place
The neuron can't repolarise back towards rest
Sodium is pumped out faster than normal
The neuron overshoots into hyperpolarisation
why: After the peak, potassium rushes out to bring the charge back down and then below rest. Without this, the neuron stays depolarised and can't repolarise or hyperpolarise. Hyperpolarisation is tempting, but it needs potassium to rush out, which the toxin prevents.

q: Three of these describe a neuron at resting potential. Which one does NOT?
opts: Sodium and potassium channels are closed
The inside is about −70 mV
Sodium is more concentrated outside
Sodium ions rush into the axon
why: Sodium rushing in is depolarisation during an action potential, not rest. Having more sodium outside is true at rest; that gradient sets the stage for a rapid action potential.

q: Three of these are jobs done by glial cells. Which one is NOT?
opts: Carrying the message from the soma to the terminals
Guiding neurons to their places in the fetal brain
Building myelin around axons in the arm
Removing viruses and fungi from brain tissue
why: Carrying the message from the soma to the axon terminals is the axon's job, which is part of the neuron. Building myelin is a glial job (Schwann cells in the PNS), as are guiding migration (radial glia) and removing microorganisms (microglia).

q: A single light tap on Aina's arm doesn't trigger a reflex, but five rapid taps on the same spot do. Which process explains this?
opts: Spatial summation
Temporal summation
An IPSP
The all-or-none law
why: Repeated stimuli at one spot over a short time add up, which is temporal summation. Spatial summation is tempting, but it needs input from several locations at once, not repeated input at one location.

q: Danial is prescribed a benzodiazepine for anxiety. It works by enhancing GABA's effect at GABA receptors. How is this drug best described?
opts: A GABA antagonist
A reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
A monoamine oxidase inhibitor
A GABA agonist
why: An agonist mimics or enhances a neurotransmitter's effect at the receptor, and benzodiazepines are GABA agonists. An antagonist is the opposite: it blocks or reduces the response.

q: A patient starts taking an MAOI. What is most likely to happen at her serotonin and dopamine synapses?
opts: More is broken down, so less stays in the synapse
Less is broken down, so more stays in the synapse
Reuptake is blocked, so it stays in the presynaptic cell
Receptors are blocked, so it can't bind
why: MAOIs block monoamine oxidase, the enzyme that breaks down serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine, so more remains available. Blocking reuptake is how SSRIs work, not MAOIs.

q: At one moment a postsynaptic neuron receives 3 EPSPs and 6 IPSPs of similar size from different synapses. What will most likely happen?
opts: It will fire, since any EPSP triggers an impulse
It will fire a weaker action potential
It won't fire, since inhibition outweighs excitation
It will fire once the IPSPs turn into EPSPs
why: Whether a neuron fires depends on the ratio of IPSPs to EPSPs at that moment, and here inhibition dominates. 'A weaker action potential' is tempting, but action potentials are all-or-none.

q: SSRIs and MAOIs both raise neurotransmitter levels in the synapse. Why is an SSRI said to act on reuptake rather than enzymatic degradation?
opts: It stops serotonin returning to the presynaptic cell
It stops enzymes from breaking serotonin down
It makes the presynaptic cell synthesise more serotonin
It mimics serotonin at the postsynaptic receptor
why: SSRIs block reuptake, so serotonin is not taken back into the presynaptic neuron. Stopping enzymes from breaking it down is enzymatic degradation, which is the MAOI mechanism.

q: Visual information must update within milliseconds. Why are ionotropic rather than metabotropic effects better suited to it?
opts: They use second messengers for lasting effects
They act through hormones carried in the blood
They open ion channels directly in under 1 ms
They take about 30 ms but last for minutes
why: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated: the neurotransmitter opens the channel immediately (< 1 ms), and the effect is brief. Second messengers and minutes-long effects describe metabotropic receptors, which suit taste, smell and attention.

q: Loewi stimulated the vagus nerve of a frog, slowing its heart, then moved the surrounding fluid to a second frog's heart, which also slowed. What did this show?
opts: Communication across the synapse is chemical
Communication across the synapse is electrical
The heart is controlled by hormones from glands
Reflexes are slower than conduction along an axon
why: A substance in the fluid alone was enough to slow the second heart, so the message was carried by a chemical (neurotransmitter). Electrical transmission was the rival idea that this experiment weakened.

q: Sherrington found that a reflex travels more slowly than an impulse along an axon, and that several weak stimuli at slightly different times give a stronger reflex than one. What did he conclude?
opts: Axons conduct impulses more slowly than expected
Reflexes are controlled by hormones in the blood
Neurons are physically joined into one network
Special processes happen at the junction between neurons
why: These delays and summation effects suggested special processes at the gap between neurons, which he named the synapse. 'Neurons are physically joined' contradicts this; the delay points to a gap, not a continuous network.

q: Encik Lim has tremors and difficulty starting movements. Doctors find too little of one neurotransmitter in brain areas that control movement. Which one?
opts: Serotonin
Dopamine
GABA
Acetylcholine
why: Too little dopamine in certain areas is linked to Parkinson's disease, and dopamine is involved in control of movement. Acetylcholine is tempting because it controls muscle contractions, but Parkinson's is linked to a dopamine shortage.

q: A patient with schizophrenia is given an antipsychotic drug. Based on how such drugs work, what does it do at the synapse?
opts: Mimics dopamine, increasing the response
Blocks serotonin reuptake, raising serotonin
Blocks dopamine receptors, reducing the response
Enhances GABA, increasing inhibition
why: Antipsychotics are dopamine antagonists, and schizophrenia is linked to too much dopamine in certain areas. Mimicking dopamine would make it an agonist, which would worsen the problem.

q: Three of these are inhibitory effects. Which one is NOT?
opts: Glutamate strengthening connections while studying
GABA reducing movement as you fall asleep
Endorphins dulling pain near the end of a run
Chloride ions entering a postsynaptic cell
why: Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter, involved in learning and plasticity. Chloride entering the cell might look neutral, but it produces an IPSP, which is a hyperpolarising brake.

q: Three of these match a hormone to its gland and effect correctly. Which one does NOT?
opts: Melatonin from the pineal gland, causing sleepiness
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex, raising blood sugar
Leptin from the pancreas, increasing appetite
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, releasing milk
why: Leptin comes from fat cells and decreases appetite; the pancreas makes insulin and glucagon. The other three pairings match the lecture's gland-by-gland list.

q: Walking home at night, Encik Lim is chased by a stray dog. His heart pounds, his pupils widen and his digestion stops. Which division is in control?
opts: Parasympathetic nervous system
Somatic nervous system
Central nervous system only
Sympathetic nervous system
why: The sympathetic division reacts to stress and prepares the body for fight-or-flight. The parasympathetic division does the opposite: it lowers heart rate and increases digestion after the threat passes.

q: Mei Ling wants to record, millisecond by millisecond, when the brain responds as people read a word. Pinpointing the exact brain location matters less. Which method suits her best?
opts: fMRI
PET
CT
EEG
why: EEG has good temporal (timing) but poor spatial resolution, which fits her goal. fMRI is tempting because it measures function in clearer detail, but it tracks slower changes in oxygenation and is chosen for location, not millisecond timing.

q: A stroke damages the motor cortex in Aina's left hemisphere. What is she most likely to experience?
opts: Weakness in the left side of her body
Weakness in the right side of her body
Loss of hearing in her left ear only
Loss of the sense of smell
why: Each hemisphere controls the opposite (contralateral) side of the body, so left motor cortex damage affects the right side. Left-side weakness would be ipsilateral, which motor control is not.

q: After surgery that removed tissue from both medial temporal lobes, Danial still remembers his childhood. What problem is he most likely to have?
opts: Forming new long-term declarative memories
Keeping his balance and coordinating movements
Regulating body temperature and hunger
Producing fluent, well-pronounced speech
why: The hippocampus in the medial temporal lobe forms long-term declarative memories, so new memories are affected while old ones remain. Balance and coordination is the cerebellum's role, not the hippocampus.

q: A patient speaks smoothly and quickly, but what she says makes no sense, and she struggles to understand others. Why is this Wernicke's aphasia rather than Broca's aphasia?
opts: Broca's patients speak fluently but without meaning
Wernicke's area is in the frontal lobe and controls speech
Broca's patients understand others but struggle to pronounce
Wernicke's patients understand others but can't speak
why: Wernicke's aphasia (left temporal lobe) gives fluent but meaningless speech with poor understanding, while Broca's aphasia (left frontal lobe) leaves understanding intact but impairs pronunciation. 'Fluent but without meaning' describes Wernicke's, not Broca's.

q: After a small tumour, a patient's body temperature, hunger and sleep-wake cycle are all disrupted, but his vision and hearing are normal. Why does this point to the hypothalamus rather than the thalamus?
opts: The thalamus regulates these drives; the hypothalamus relays senses
The hypothalamus regulates these drives; the thalamus relays senses
The hypothalamus is in the hindbrain and controls breathing
The thalamus only relays smell, which is unaffected here
why: The hypothalamus regulates temperature, eating, drinking and sleep-wake cycles, while the thalamus is the relay station for most senses, so thalamic damage would reduce sensation. The last option is wrong because smell is the one sense that does not pass through the thalamus.

q: After an iron rod injured his left prefrontal cortex, Phineas Gage became impulsive and lost his inhibition, though he survived. What does this case support?
opts: The PFC is responsible for sensing touch and temperature
The PFC controls balance and coordination of movement
The PFC regulates self-control and impulsive behaviour
The PFC is the brain's relay station for senses
why: Gage's change in personality and loss of inhibition supports the PFC's role in executive functions such as self-control. Touch and temperature belong to the parietal lobe, not the frontal lobe.

q: In a lesioning study, rats with a small region near the hippocampus destroyed stop showing fear responses to a tone that used to signal shock. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: The cerebellum stores conditioned fear habits
The thalamus produces emotional responses
The medulla controls fearful behaviour
The amygdala is involved in fear and fear memory
why: The almond-shaped amygdala near the hippocampus is responsible for fear responses and fear memory. The cerebellum is tempting because it stores learned reflexes and habits, but the region described is the amygdala, and fear is its job.

q: After a fall onto the back of his head, Danial becomes clumsy, loses his balance and slurs his speech. Which structure was most likely damaged?
opts: Medulla
Basal ganglia
Cerebellum
Occipital lobe
why: Cerebellum damage causes clumsiness, poor balance, slurred speech and timing difficulty. The occipital lobe is also at the back of the head, but damage there would affect vision, not balance.

q: A neck injury damages the lowest part of the brain, just above the spinal cord. Doctors immediately put the patient on a breathing machine. Which structure was injured?
opts: Pons
Cerebellum
Reticular formation
Medulla
why: The medulla, the first swelling at the top of the spinal cord, controls life-sustaining functions such as breathing and heart rate. The pons is tempting because it sits just above the medulla, but it is involved in sleep, dreaming and arousal.

q: Three of these are controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Which one is NOT?
opts: Pupils widening during a scary movie
Choosing to kick a football towards the goal
Stomach digesting a plate of nasi lemak
Heart rate slowing while resting at home
why: Kicking a ball is a voluntary muscle movement, controlled by the somatic nervous system. Pupil changes, digestion and heart rate are involuntary, so they are all autonomic.

q: Three of these brain methods are noninvasive. Which one is NOT?
opts: Deep brain stimulation
Transcranial magnetic stimulation
Transcranial direct current stimulation
Electroencephalography
why: Deep brain stimulation is invasive: it uses an implanted generator and electrodes. tDCS also uses electric current, but the very low current is passed through scalp electrodes, so it is noninvasive.

q: On the LRT, Aina notices that nearby lamp posts rush past while distant hills seem to drift by slowly. Which depth cue is she using?
opts: Linear perspective
Relative size
Binocular disparity
Motion parallax
why: Close objects appearing to move faster than far ones is motion parallax. Relative size is tempting, but it is based on how small an object looks, not how fast it seems to move.

q: Encik Lim bangs his elbow on a table and immediately rubs it, and the pain eases. Which theory best explains this?
opts: Gate-control theory of pain
Opponent-process theory
Sensory adaptation
Subliminal perception
why: Gate-control theory says non-pain signals, such as rubbing, can close the spinal 'gate' that pain signals must pass through. Sensory adaptation is tempting, but it takes time with an unchanging stimulus and doesn't explain an instant reduction from rubbing.

q: Mei Ling stares at a bright green square for 60 seconds and then looks at a white wall. What will she most likely see, and why?
opts: A green afterimage, as green cones keep firing
A blue afterimage, as blue and green are opponents
A red afterimage, as fatigued green cells let red dominate
No afterimage, as white light hits all cones equally
why: In opponent-process theory, staring at green fatigues green cells; on white, the opponent red cells are more active, so she sees red. Blue is tempting, but the opponent pairs are red–green and blue–yellow.

q: At a dimly lit night market, Danial can make out the shapes of stalls but struggles to tell the colours of the shirts on sale. What best explains this?
opts: Cones dominate in dim light and code only shapes
The blind spot widens when light levels drop
Sensory adaptation switches off colour receptors
Rods dominate in dim light and don't code colour
why: Rods work well in dim light but give non-colour vision, while cones need bright light for colour. The second option is wrong because it reverses the roles of rods and cones.

q: After a few minutes, Puan Siti no longer hears the classroom aircon, although her ears still respond to it. Why is this habituation rather than sensory adaptation?
opts: Her receptors stop sending signals to her brain
The hum falls below her absolute threshold
The sound becomes a subliminal stimulus
Her brain stops attending, though receptors still signal
why: In habituation, the brain stops attending to constant information that is still being received. In sensory adaptation, the receptor cells themselves stop responding, which doesn't fit here because her ears still respond.

q: A kopitiam owner slowly adds more sugar to a cup of teh. A customer can tell this cup is sweeter than the usual cup only half the time. Why is this a just noticeable difference, not an absolute threshold?
opts: It is detected 50% of the time, not every time
It involves taste, not vision or hearing
It compares two stimuli, not detecting one at all
It is below conscious awareness, not above it
why: A JND is the smallest difference between two stimuli detected 50% of the time; an absolute threshold is the lowest level of a single stimulus that can be detected. The 50% option is tempting, but both thresholds use the 50% rule, so it can't tell them apart.

q: Researchers find visual neurons that are excited by red light and inhibited by green light, and others excited by blue and inhibited by yellow. Which theory does this most directly support?
opts: Trichromatic theory
Opponent-process theory
Gate-control theory
Gestalt principle of similarity
why: Neurons stimulated by one colour and inhibited by its partner in red–green and blue–yellow pairs is Hering's opponent-process theory. Trichromatic theory is tempting, but it is about three cone types sensitive to ranges of wavelengths, not opposing pairs.

q: Students shown a list of letters read an ambiguous symbol as 'B', while students shown a list of numbers read the same symbol as '13'. What does this finding demonstrate?
opts: Perceptual set and top-down processing
Bottom-up processing of small features
Sensory adaptation to repeated stimuli
The Gestalt principle of closure
why: What they expected to see from previous context shaped what they perceived, which is perceptual set driven by top-down knowledge. Bottom-up processing is the reverse: it builds a perception from features alone, so it can't explain why the same features were read differently.

q: A stroke damages Aina's right visual cortex. Which part of her vision is most likely to be lost?
opts: Her right visual field
Colour vision in both eyes
Only her blind spot
Her left visual field
why: The visual pathway is contralateral: the left visual field is processed by the right visual cortex. Losing the right visual field would follow damage to the left visual cortex.

q: After thalamus damage, a patient's sight, hearing and touch are partly lost, yet his sense of smell is normal. What best explains this?
opts: Smell signals reach the olfactory bulbs without the thalamus
Smell is processed by the thalamus on the opposite side
Olfactory receptors are protected inside the cochlea
Smell is a skin sense carried by free nerve endings
why: Most sensory information passes through the thalamus, but olfactory signals go straight to the olfactory bulbs and then to the piriform and orbitofrontal cortex. The other options misplace smell entirely.

q: Three of these are monocular depth cues. Which one is NOT?
opts: Railway tracks seeming to meet far away
The difference between your two eyes' images
A car blocking part of a lorry behind it
Grass looking finer further across a field
why: The difference between the two eyes' images is binocular disparity, which needs both eyes. The others are linear perspective, overlap and texture gradient, which all work with one eye.

q: Three of these are Gestalt principles of perceptual organisation. Which one is NOT?
opts: The moon looking larger on the horizon
Seeing a broken circle as a full circle
Seeing a dashed line as one smooth path
Grouping students by matching uniforms
why: The moon looking larger on the horizon is a perceptual illusion caused by comparison with buildings, not a grouping principle. The others are closure, continuity and similarity.

q: Danial is scolded by his manager for arriving late after an LRT breakdown. He says nothing at work, but that evening he shouts at his younger brother for leaving shoes at the door. Which defence mechanism best explains his outburst?
opts: Rationalisation
Displacement
Repression
Sublimation
why: His anger is redirected onto a safer target (his brother) who did not cause it, which is displacement. Rationalisation would mean inventing an acceptable excuse, not shifting anger onto someone else.

q: After failing her SPM trial Add Maths paper, Mei Ling tells everyone, "The paper was unfair, and I don't need that subject for psychology anyway." Why is this rationalisation rather than denial?
opts: She refuses to acknowledge that she failed the paper at all
She pushes the memory of failing out of conscious awareness
She redirects her disappointment onto the exam setters
She admits she failed but makes up acceptable excuses for it
why: Rationalisation means accepting the event happened but inventing acceptable reasons for it. Denial would require her to refuse to recognise the failure, yet she openly mentions it.

q: Seven-year-old Haziq sees the last piece of kuih on the table but does not take it. Which reason would show that his SUPERego, rather than his ego, is in control?
opts: His mother is watching and he does not want to be scolded
He plans to take it later when nobody is in the kitchen
He would feel guilty because taking it without asking is wrong
He has just eaten, so he does not really want it now
why: Guilt from knowing an act is wrong comes from the conscience, part of the superego. Avoiding a scolding is the ego's reality principle: it blocks the id only because of negative consequences.

q: A baby is weaned from breastfeeding very suddenly and harshly at eight months, leaving the conflict unresolved. According to Freud, which adult pattern is this person most likely to show?
opts: Being extremely tidy, stubborn and stingy
Chain smoking, nail biting or overeating
Promiscuous sexual behaviour in relationships
Seeing the opposite sex as "awful" in adulthood
why: Weaning is the conflict of the oral stage (first 18 months), and oral fixation shows as mouth-focused habits. Tidiness and stinginess describe an anal-retentive fixation from toilet training conflicts.

q: A researcher tries to test whether unresolved oral conflict causes smoking. She realises that whether a person smokes or not, a Freudian could explain the result using hidden unconscious motives. Which criticism of psychodynamic theory does this best illustrate?
opts: Its sample was limited to wealthy Victorian women
Behaviourists say it ignores observable behaviour
It is idealistic and more philosophical than scientific
It is too ambiguous and therefore hard to falsify
why: If every possible outcome can be explained, the theory cannot be proven wrong, which is the ambiguity/falsifiability criticism. The limited-sample criticism is about who Freud studied, not about untestable predictions.

q: Kai believes he is bad at public speaking, so he avoids volunteering for class presentations. His groupmates stop asking him to present, which makes him feel even less capable. Which concept best explains this cycle?
opts: Bandura's reciprocal determinism
Rotter's external locus of control
Rogers' conditional positive regard
Trait-situation interaction
why: His beliefs (cognition), his avoidance (behaviour) and his groupmates' reactions (environment) keep influencing one another, which is reciprocal determinism. External locus of control would require him to blame fate or others for outcomes, which he does not.

q: Aina and Danial have similar presentation skills. Aina has succeeded at past presentations and her lecturer often praises her; Danial has failed several before. Both are given a difficult new presentation. What does Bandura's theory predict?
opts: Aina will try harder and persist longer because of higher self-efficacy
Both will try equally hard because their actual skills are similar
Danial will persist longer because he has more to prove this time
Aina will give up sooner because past success makes her careless
why: Self-efficacy depends on past experience and perceived competence from self and others, and higher self-efficacy leads to more effort. Equal skill is not enough, because expectancy of success, not just ability, drives effort.

q: Farah says, "Whether I get the scholarship depends entirely on luck and on whether the panel likes my face." Which concept fits her statement best, and why?
opts: Low self-efficacy: she doubts her own skill at the interview tasks
Low reinforcement value: she prefers other rewards to the scholarship
External locus of control: she credits outcomes to fate and other people
Conditional regard: she feels valued only when others approve of her
why: Attributing outcomes to luck and other people's choices is an external locus of control. Low self-efficacy is tempting, but she never says she lacks ability; she says her actions do not decide the result.

q: Jun sees himself as an average student and a shy club member, but he believes he SHOULD be the top scorer and a confident club president. According to Rogers, what is most likely?
opts: He will become a fully functioning person
He will feel competent and capable most of the time
He will experience anxiety and neurotic behaviour
He will reach self-actualisation more quickly
why: A large mismatch between the real self and the ideal self produces anxiety and neurotic behaviour. Feeling competent and capable comes from a close match, which Jun does not have.

q: Mei Ling scores very high on extraversion. She tells jokes and chats loudly at her friend's birthday party but stays quiet and subdued at a funeral wake the next day. Which idea best explains this?
opts: Introversion as a source trait
Low conscientiousness
Reciprocal determinism
Trait-situation interaction
why: Her trait is stable, but the situation shapes how it is expressed, which is trait-situation interaction. Calling her introverted ignores that her extraversion shows strongly whenever the setting allows it.

q: Studies in many countries and languages find the same five personality factors, and people's self-ratings largely match ratings by people who know them. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: Personality structure is set mainly by the culture a person grows up in
The Big Five are broadly consistent across cultures, with some regional variation
The five factors are strongly dependent on and overlap with one another
Cattell's 16 source traits are the most universal description of personality
why: Consistency across regions, languages and self/observer ratings supports the Big Five as largely universal, though regional variations still exist. If culture set personality structure, the factors would differ between cultures, not repeat.

q: Three of these people show sublimation. Which one does NOT?
opts: A teenager with strong aggressive urges becomes a skilled boxer
A person who loves attention becomes a stage performer instead
A worker angry at his boss comes home and kicks the family cat
Someone with violent impulses channels them into competitive rugby
why: Sublimation turns unacceptable urges into socially acceptable activities. Kicking the cat redirects anger onto an innocent target, which is displacement, not an acceptable outlet.

q: Three of these give a behavioural or social cognitive explanation of someone's personality. Which one does NOT?
opts: Sara became shy because speaking up in class was often punished
Wei's aggression is traced to an unresolved conflict in the phallic stage
Ravi became polite after watching his sister get praised for politeness
Nina studies hard because she expects that effort will be rewarded
why: Explaining personality through unresolved psychosexual conflict is psychodynamic. The others use operant conditioning, observational learning and expectancy, which are behavioural or social cognitive ideas.

q: Three of these show CONDITIONAL positive regard. Which one does NOT?
opts: A father praises his daughter only when she brings home straight As
A coach is warm to a player only after the team has won a match
A grandmother is affectionate only when the grandchildren visit her
A mother tells her son she loves him whatever his SPM results are
why: Love given with no strings attached is unconditional positive regard, which Rogers says is needed to reach full potential. The other three give regard only when the provider's expectations are met.

q: In a company, junior staff never question the director, and everyone expects that major decisions will be made by a few people at the top. Staff see this as normal and fair. Which Hofstede dimension does this reflect?
opts: High collectivism
High uncertainty avoidance
High masculinity
High power distance
why: Power distance is how much less powerful members accept and expect that power is held by a few. Collectivism involves respect for hierarchy too, but its core is group duty and loyalty rather than accepting unequal power.

q: Country X has very detailed laws, strict safety regulations, and little tolerance for opinions that differ from the accepted truth. Why does this point to high uncertainty avoidance rather than collectivism?
opts: It shows that people value duty, tradition and group status
It shows low tolerance of ambiguity and unstructured situations
It shows that people accept power being held by a small elite
It shows that people value being assertive and competitive
why: Strict rules, many safety measures and belief in One Truth are signs of low tolerance for uncertainty. Duty, tradition and group status describe collectivism, which the scenario never mentions.

q: Identical twins separated at birth both enjoyed carpentry, smoked and drank similar amounts, and each divorced a Linda and married a Betty. Which conclusion does this case support best?
opts: Genes may strongly shape personality and preferences
Environment plays no role at all in personality
Personality can be read from the shape of the skull
Shared family environment explains their similarity
why: The "Jim" twins share genes but were raised apart, so their similarities point to genetic influence. It cannot show environment plays no role, since both were raised in Ohio by parents of similar socioeconomic background.

q: A participant scores very high on neuroticism. Based on DeYoung et al. (2010), which MRI pattern is most likely?
opts: Larger medial orbitofrontal cortex in the reward-value area
Larger dorsomedial prefrontal cortex; smaller middle cingulate
Smaller dorsomedial prefrontal cortex; larger middle cingulate cortex
A visible skull bulge over the area for anxious emotions
why: Neuroticism was linked to less volume in threat and negative-emotion areas and more in the error-detection and pain area (middle cingulate). A larger medial orbitofrontal cortex was linked to extraversion, not neuroticism.

q: Researchers compare shyness in identical twins raised in different homes with shyness in unrelated adopted children raised in the same home. Based on twin and adoption studies, what result is most likely?
opts: The twins raised apart will be more alike in shyness
The adopted siblings will be more alike in shyness
Both pairs will be about equally alike in shyness
Neither pair will show any similarity in shyness
why: Twin and adoption studies suggest genes account for much of personality, including shyness, regardless of shared environment. Shared home environment alone would predict the adopted siblings being more alike, which the evidence does not support.

q: A school psychologist sits at the back of a Year 2 class and records how many times Amir leaves his seat during a 30-minute lesson. Which type of assessment is this?
opts: Personality inventory using standard statements
Projective test using ambiguous stimuli
Semi-structured interview with follow-ups
Behavioural assessment using a frequency count
why: Counting how often a behaviour occurs in a set time is a frequency count, a behavioural assessment. A personality inventory relies on self-report answers, whereas here Amir reports nothing himself.

q: A client is shown an ambiguous picture of a woman standing at a window and asked to tell a story about what led up to the scene and what happens next. Why is this the TAT rather than the Rorschach?
opts: The client makes up a story about people in a picture
The client says what an inkblot shape looks like
The client answers true/false to a fixed list of items
The client is rated on how often a behaviour occurs
why: The TAT uses ambiguous pictures of people and asks for a story, looking for projected problems. Both are projective tests, but the Rorschach uses inkblots and asks only what each looks like.

q: Encik Lim applies for a bank job and must complete a personality inventory as part of screening. Which problem is most likely to affect his answers?
opts: The interviewer may judge him by one good first impression
He may give socially acceptable answers to look good
His behaviour may change because he knows he is observed
The scorer may interpret his answers very subjectively
why: A known weakness of self-report inventories is that people give socially acceptable answers, especially when a job is at stake. A halo effect from an interviewer is a limitation of interviews, not of standardised questionnaires.

q: Three of these describe completing a personality inventory. Which one does NOT?
opts: Responding to 335 statements with built-in validity scales
Rating 240 items that cover five main personality dimensions
Answering a questionnaire that sorts you into 16 types
Telling a story about each of 20 ambiguous pictures
why: Telling stories about ambiguous pictures is the TAT, a projective test. The others describe the MMPI-3, NEO-PI-3 and MBTI, which are standardised questionnaires.

q: A company uses the MBTI to decide who gets promoted. Research shows many people get a different four-letter type when they retake it a few weeks later. What does this finding suggest?
opts: The MBTI measures abnormal behaviour rather than normal personality
Personality traits change completely within a few weeks
The MBTI is a projective test, so its scoring is subjective
The MBTI has limited reliability, so it is a weak basis for decisions
why: Getting different results on retest is a reliability problem, and the MBTI is known for limited validity and reliability. It is a self-report inventory, not a projective test, so subjective scoring is not the explanation.

q: In a lab study, a rat's ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) is damaged. What is the most likely result?
opts: It overeats and gains a lot of weight
It stops eating unless it is force-fed
It eats normally because leptin takes over
It eats only when its insulin levels rise
why: The VMH may stop eating when glucose rises, so damage removes this brake and leads to overeating. Stopping eating unless force-fed is the effect of lateral hypothalamus damage.

q: Mice with a gene mutation cannot produce leptin. Which outcome would you predict?
opts: They stop eating because the hypothalamus thinks they are full
They keep eating and become obese, as fullness is not signalled
Their blood glucose rises because the pancreas makes no insulin
Their weight set point drops and they become very thin
why: Leptin tells the hypothalamus there is "enough food", reducing appetite and increasing fullness, so without it appetite stays high. Blood glucose control is the job of insulin and glucagon from the pancreas, not leptin.

q: A student living in a shelter is struggling to find regular meals and a safe place to sleep. A counsellor's talk on discovering his life purpose has little effect on him. Which theory best explains this?
opts: Self-determination theory
Maslow's hierarchy of needs
McClelland's need theory
Arousal theory
why: Maslow argued deficiency needs such as food and safety must be met before growth needs like self-actualisation. Self-determination theory focuses on autonomy, competence and relatedness, not on basic survival needs coming first.

q: Aina is sitting a very difficult SPM Additional Mathematics paper and is extremely anxious, with her heart racing. According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, what is most likely?
opts: She performs better, since higher arousal always helps
She performs best, since hard tasks suit high arousal
She performs worse, since hard tasks suit low-moderate arousal
Her arousal has no effect, since the paper is so hard
why: Moderate arousal gives the best performance, and difficult tasks need low-moderate arousal, so very high anxiety hurts her. High-moderate arousal suits easy tasks, not difficult ones.

q: Danial has eaten, slept well and has no pressing needs, yet he spends his holiday skydiving and bungee jumping because he feels restless when life is calm. Which theory best explains his behaviour?
opts: Drive-reduction theory
Instinct approach
Self-determination theory
Arousal theory
why: Arousal theory says people keep an optimal level of tension, and sensation seekers increase stimulation to reach it. Drive-reduction theory cannot explain seeking MORE arousal when no physiological need is present.

q: Lina chooses group projects so she can work with friends, avoids arguments, and turns down a team-leader role because it would mean criticising teammates. Which of McClelland's needs is strongest in her?
opts: Need for achievement (nAch)
Need for power (nPow)
Need for affiliation (nAff)
Need for competence (SDT)
why: Her choices centre on friendly relationships and avoiding conflict, which is nAff. She turns down a chance to influence others, which goes against a strong need for power.

q: Siew Ling believes her intelligence is fixed and that grades mostly depend on luck. She fails her first psychology midterm. According to Dweck, how is she most likely to respond?
opts: Study harder, believing effort will help
Give up, believing she lacks the ability
Seek out harder tasks to test her limits
Ask for feedback to master the topic
why: Dweck linked a fixed view of intelligence and an external locus to low achievement motivation, so failure leads to giving up. Increasing effort fits someone who sees intelligence as changeable and has an internal locus.

q: Encik Lim plays chess at the community hall every evening, even though there are no prizes and nobody watches. Why is this intrinsic rather than extrinsic motivation?
opts: He plays to reduce the tension of a physiological need
He plays to earn praise and approval from other players
He plays because an external reward lures him into action
Playing the game is itself what he finds rewarding
why: Intrinsic motivation means the act itself is rewarding. Playing for praise or another external reward would be extrinsic, because the outcome is separate from the activity.

q: Aina has not drunk any water all day after futsal. Her body's requirement for water is the ____, and the uncomfortable tension that pushes her to buy a drink is the ____.
opts: drive; need
need; drive
incentive; need
drive; homeostasis
why: A need is the requirement for something essential to survival, and a drive is the tension and arousal that the need creates. Swapping them is the common error: the drive is what motivates action, not the requirement itself.

q: In a study, students who chose their own assignment topics and received supportive feedback showed more interest in the work than students given strict instructions and controlling deadlines. Which theory does this support best?
opts: Self-determination theory
Drive-reduction theory
Yerkes-Dodson law
Instinct approach
why: Self-determination theory says a supportive context that meets needs for autonomy and competence increases intrinsic motivation. Drive-reduction deals with reducing physiological tension, which is not what the study manipulated.

q: Three of these are driven by acquired (secondary) drives. Which one is NOT?
opts: Working overtime to earn more money for a new phone
Posting photos on Instagram to get likes and comments
Drinking two bottles of water after a long futsal match
Studying hard so that parents will praise the results
why: Thirst after exercise is a primary drive based on the body's survival needs. Money, likes and praise are learned through experience or conditioning, so they are acquired drives.

q: Three of these behaviours are hard for drive-reduction theory to explain. Which one fits drive-reduction theory well?
opts: Ordering cendol for dessert after a full dinner
Going rock climbing just for the thrill of it
Eating a big plate of rice after fasting all day
Doing puzzles for fun when not bored or hungry
why: Eating after a long fast reduces the tension of a real physiological need, exactly what drive-reduction predicts. Eating when not hungry and seeking extra arousal are the classic limits of drive-reduction theory.

q: After surgery that damaged her amygdala, a patient is shown photos of faces. Which difficulty is she most likely to have?
opts: Recalling the names of people she has just met
Feeling her heart beat faster during exercise
Recognising fear in other people's facial expressions
Choosing to distract herself from upsetting thoughts
why: The amygdala is linked to fear and helps identify facial expressions, so damage impairs recognising fear in faces. Distraction as a regulation strategy is linked to the anterior cingulate cortex, not the amygdala.

q: Brain scans show that Haris has noticeably more activity in his right frontal lobe than his left. Based on Davidson (2003), what would you predict about him?
opts: He tends to experience more positive emotions
He has trouble reading emotion from faces
He tends to experience more negative emotions
He reacts to threats before conscious awareness
why: Davidson linked left frontal activity with positive emotions and right frontal activity with negative emotions. Reading emotion from faces is a right-hemisphere ability, so more right activity would not make that harder.

q: Before a scholarship interview, Aina tells herself, "This is just a chance to practise, not a test of my worth," and feels calmer. Which brain area and effect best fit this strategy?
opts: Lateral orbitofrontal cortex; reduced amygdala activity
Anterior cingulate cortex; reduced amygdala activity
Lateral orbitofrontal cortex; increased amygdala activity
Left frontal lobe; increased sympathetic arousal
why: Reinterpreting the situation is reappraisal, linked to the lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and it lowers amygdala activity. The anterior cingulate cortex is linked to distraction, a different regulation strategy.

q: On a jungle trail at FRIM, Danial jumps back from a curved shape on the path. A moment later he realises it is only a stick. Which process explains why he jumped BEFORE recognising the object?
opts: The low road to the amygdala
The high road to the amygdala
The facial feedback hypothesis
Cognitive appraisal (Lazarus)
why: The low road is a fast, crude subcortical route that triggers a reaction before conscious awareness. The high road is the slower cortical route that let him recognise it was "only a stick".

q: After three cups of kopi, Mei Ling's heart is pounding. She sits beside an attractive classmate and decides she must be falling for him. Why does Schachter and Singer's theory explain this better than James-Lange?
opts: Her bodily arousal comes before she feels the emotion
Her thalamus triggers arousal and emotion at the same time
She labels general arousal using cues in her surroundings
Her smiling face sends feedback that intensifies emotion
why: Two-factor theory needs both arousal and a label taken from environmental cues, and she uses the classmate as the cue. Arousal coming before emotion is true of both theories, so it does not tell them apart.

q: People with spinal cord injuries, who receive little feedback from their bodies, report feeling emotions as strongly as before their injury. Which theory does this finding most directly weaken?
opts: Cannon-Bard theory
Cognitive-mediational theory
James-Lange theory
Common sense theory
why: James-Lange says emotion is the interpretation of bodily arousal, so less bodily feedback should mean weaker emotion. Cannon-Bard actually fits this finding, since it says emotion does not depend on first sensing bodily changes.

q: Participants held a pen between their teeth, which forces a smile, or between their lips, which blocks one. The "smiling" group rated cartoons as funnier. Which theory does this support?
opts: Cannon-Bard theory
Common sense theory
Facial feedback hypothesis
Cognitive-mediational theory
why: Strack et al. (1988) showed that facial expressions feed back to the brain and intensify emotion. Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion occur together from the thalamus, with no role for facial muscles causing emotion.

q: Two students receive the same email from their lecturer: "Please see me in my office tomorrow." Afiq thinks he is about to be praised; Wen thinks he is in trouble. According to Lazarus, what will happen?
opts: They will feel the same emotion because the email is identical
They will feel different emotions because they appraise it differently
They will feel the same emotion once their arousal levels match
They will feel no emotion until their faces show an expression
why: Lazarus said appraisal of a stimulus comes first and determines the emotion, so different interpretations give different emotions. Assuming the same stimulus produces the same emotion is the common sense view, which ignores appraisal.

q: Encik Lim's car skids on a wet highway. He later says, "My heart started racing at the exact moment I felt afraid; neither came first." Which theory matches his experience?
opts: James-Lange theory
Schachter-Singer theory
Cognitive-mediational theory
Cannon-Bard theory
why: Cannon-Bard holds that the thalamus signals the cortex and the sympathetic nervous system at the same time, so arousal and emotion are simultaneous. James-Lange would put the racing heart first, with fear following.

q: Researchers ask an elderly, traditional Chinese-Malaysian grandmother and her highly Westernised granddaughter to describe what love feels like. Based on Tsai et al. (2004), what is most likely?
opts: The grandmother will use more direct emotion words
The grandmother will use more bodily or social words
Both will use the same words, as emotions are universal
The granddaughter will use more bodily or social words
why: Tsai et al. found traditional Chinese Americans described emotion with bodily or social words, while Americanised groups used direct emotion words like "love". Facial expressions may be universal, but labelling emotion is learned and shaped by language and culture.

q: Danial is walking home alone late at night and hears footsteps behind him. Three of these are signs of sympathetic arousal. Which one is NOT?
opts: His heart rate rises sharply and quickly
He starts breathing much faster
His pupils dilate to let in more light
His pupils shrink and digestion speeds up
why: The sympathetic nervous system raises heart rate, speeds breathing and dilates the pupils. Constricted pupils and faster digestion are signs of a calm, resting state, the opposite of arousal.

q: Puan Siti tells her class, "We do not cry because we are sad; we feel sad because we cry." Which theory is she describing, and why is it not common sense theory?
opts: Common sense: the emotion is felt first and then causes the crying
Cannon-Bard: crying and sadness are triggered together by the thalamus
Lazarus: the situation must be appraised before crying can occur
James-Lange: the bodily reaction comes first and is labelled as emotion
why: James-Lange reverses the common sense order: arousal or a bodily reaction comes first, and interpreting it produces the emotion. Common sense theory puts emotion before the physical reaction, which is exactly what she rejects.

q: Uncle Ah Kow left school at 15 and scored poorly on exams, but he runs a busy kopitiam, reads customers well and always negotiates good deals with suppliers. In Sternberg's theory, which intelligence is he strongest in?
opts: Analytical intelligence
Creative intelligence
Practical intelligence
Crystallised intelligence
why: Practical intelligence is using information to get along and succeed in real life, like running a business and handling people. Analytical intelligence is breaking problems into parts, the kind of skill school exams test, where he did poorly.

q: Madam Wong, a 70-year-old retired teacher, beats her grandchildren at vocabulary games but is much slower than them at solving unfamiliar logic puzzles. Which explanation fits CHC theory?
opts: Her fluid intelligence is strong; her crystallised intelligence is weaker
Her general g factor is high, so all of her abilities must be equal
Her crystallised intelligence is strong; her fluid intelligence is weaker
Her practical intelligence is strong; her analytical intelligence is weak
why: Vocabulary reflects crystallised intelligence (acquired knowledge), while new puzzles need fluid intelligence (problem solving in unfamiliar situations). Swapping the two is the common error: knowledge is crystallised, novel reasoning is fluid.

q: A 10-year-old scores 68 on an IQ test but dresses himself, has friends and handles daily tasks as well as his classmates. Why should he NOT be diagnosed with intellectual disability on this result alone?
opts: Diagnosis requires an IQ score below 50 at the very least
Diagnosis also needs severe deficits in adaptive behaviour
Diagnosis can only be made once a person reaches adulthood
Diagnosis requires a known genetic cause like Down syndrome
why: Intellectual disability requires an IQ below 70 AND severely deficient adaptive behaviour for one's age. A low score alone is not enough; the cutoff is 70, not 50, so his score is not the issue.

q: Using Terman's ratio formula, an 8-year-old girl answers questions at the level of an average 10-year-old. What is her IQ?
why: IQ = mental age / chronological age x 100, so 10 / 8 x 100 = 125. Choosing 80 comes from dividing the wrong way round (8 / 10 x 100).

q: On a maths reasoning test, Kumar scores far above his classmates. According to Spearman's theory, how is he most likely to do on verbal and spatial tests?
opts: Below average, because strength in one area costs another
Average, because each ability is completely independent
Unpredictable, because only specific (s) abilities exist
Above average, because one general ability underlies all of them
why: Spearman's g factor means superiority in one area predicts superiority overall. The idea that abilities are fully independent is closer to Gardner's view, not Spearman's.

q: Across several modernised countries, average IQ scores have risen steadily over decades, far faster than genes could change. Which conclusion does this best support?
opts: IQ is fixed by genes and cannot be changed
IQ tests are biased toward the test designer's culture
Environmental factors can strongly influence IQ scores
Intelligence is best described by a single g factor
why: The Flynn effect happens too quickly to be genetic, so it points to environmental influences. Cultural bias concerns differences between groups taking the same test, not rising scores over time.

q: Twin and adoption studies find IQ correlations rise as genetic relatedness increases, with heritability of about 0.50. What is the most accurate conclusion?
opts: Environment has very little effect on a person's IQ
Exactly half of each person's IQ points come from their genes
IQ is mostly determined by schooling and family income
Genes and environment each account for a large share of IQ variation
why: Heritability of about 50% means genes explain roughly half of the IQ variation in a population, leaving the rest to environment. It describes a population, so it does not mean half of one individual's IQ points come from genes.

q: Students who were reminded of a negative stereotype about their group just before an IQ test scored lower than similar students who were not reminded. What does this finding show?
opts: Group differences in IQ are mainly due to heredity
IQ tests use content that favours the designer's culture
Situational pressure can lower test scores, separate from ability
IQ scores have been rising steadily across generations
why: This is stereotype threat: knowing a negative stereotype can make people score poorly. It challenges Bell Curve-style hereditary claims, since the same students scored differently depending only on the reminder.

q: A company's new aptitude test gives almost identical scores when employees retake it a month later, but scores turn out to depend on typing speed rather than reasoning ability. How should the test be described?
opts: Valid but not reliable
Both reliable and valid
Neither reliable nor valid
Reliable but not valid
why: Consistent scores across retests show reliability, but measuring typing speed instead of reasoning means it is not measuring what it should, so it lacks validity. Being consistent does not make a test valid.

q: After a stroke, a patient shows the largest drop in working memory and in solving new reasoning problems. Scans show damage to frontal and parietal areas. Which theory best predicts this pattern?
opts: Gardner's multiple intelligences
Sternberg's triarchic theory
Parieto-Frontal Integration Theory (P-FIT)
Spearman's g factor theory
why: P-FIT names frontal and parietal areas as key to intelligence and links working memory to fluid intelligence. Spearman's theory describes a general ability but does not locate it in specific brain areas.

q: A test is given to a child who grew up in a rural Sarawak longhouse. Three of these items are likely to be culturally biased. Which one is closest to culture-fair?
opts: Explaining what people do at an ice-skating rink
Naming the author of the play Romeo and Juliet
Describing how to buy a ticket for a subway train
Choosing the shape that completes an abstract pattern
why: Culture-fair tests such as Raven's Progressive Matrices use non-verbal abstract reasoning. The other items depend on language and content from a particular culture the child may never have met.

q: Three of these show high emotional intelligence. Which one does NOT?
opts: Noticing a quiet friend is upset and gently checking in
Calming her own nerves before an exam to think clearly
Solving a difficult logic puzzle faster than anyone else
Using frustration about a failure to push toward a goal
why: Emotional intelligence is being aware of and managing your own emotions and understanding others' feelings. Solving a logic puzzle quickly reflects fluid reasoning, not emotional skills.

q: Mei Ling has to memorise a 12-digit tracking number for a parcel. Instead of repeating it digit by digit, she splits it into three groups of four and remembers them as 'her birth year', 'her house number' and 'her old locker code'. What is she mainly doing to keep it in short-term memory?
opts: Chunking it into fewer, meaningful units
Relying on echoic memory of the digits
Using state-dependent retrieval cues
Maintenance rehearsal of each single digit
why: Grouping 12 digits into 3 meaningful units fits Miller's 7 ± 2 capacity limit — that is chunking. Maintenance rehearsal would just mean repeating the digits over and over, which is exactly what she avoided.

q: Aina bumps into a girl at Mid Valley and cannot recall her name at all. A week later, back at her old tuition centre in Cheras where they studied together, the name suddenly comes to her. Which concept best explains this?
opts: Context-dependent encoding specificity
The recency effect in serial position
Automatic encoding of a flashbulb event
State-dependent encoding specificity
why: The physical place where the information was learned (the tuition centre) acted as a retrieval cue — context-dependent memory. State-dependent memory would involve matching an internal physiological or emotional state, not a location.

q: Encik Lim can still describe exactly which kopitiam he was sitting in, what he was drinking and who was beside him when he heard shocking, unexpected news about a family member years ago — even though he never tried to memorise any of it. What best explains this?
opts: Semantic memory of a widely known fact
A flashbulb memory formed by automatic encoding
Eidetic imagery held in iconic memory
Elaborative rehearsal linking it to old knowledge
why: An unexpected event with strong emotion entered LTM with little or no effortful encoding — a flashbulb memory. Elaborative rehearsal is tempting, but that requires deliberate effort to make information meaningful, which he never did.

q: A lecturer reads out a list of 15 unrelated words once, then asks HELP students to write down as many as they can immediately. Which words are students most likely to FORGET?
opts: Words from the very beginning of the list
Words from the middle of the list
Words from the very end of the list
Words from the beginning and end equally
why: The serial position effect predicts good recall for the start (primacy) and end (recency) of a list, so the middle items are forgotten most. Beginning and end items are the best remembered, not the worst.

q: Three groups see the same 40 words. Group A counts the vowels in each word, Group B decides what each word rhymes with, and Group C decides whether each word describes something alive. All are then given a surprise recall test. What result is most likely?
opts: C recalls most, B next, A least
All three groups recall about the same
B recalls most because STM is auditory
A recalls most, B next, C least
why: The levels-of-processing model predicts that deeper (semantic) processing produces better memory than phonemic (rhyme), which beats shallow visual processing (vowel counting). STM's auditory encoding doesn't make rhyme judgements the deepest level.

q: Puan Siti changed her mobile number last month. When a clerk asks for her number, she keeps reciting her OLD number by mistake. Which type of interference is this, and why?
opts: Proactive — old information is blocking retrieval of the new
Retroactive — the new number came after the old number
Retroactive — new information is blocking retrieval of the old
Proactive — the new number is erasing the old memory trace
why: The older number is interfering with retrieving the newer one, which is proactive interference. It would only be retroactive if the new number were making her unable to remember the old one.

q: Danial gets most MCQ questions right but goes blank on short-answer questions about the same topics. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: MCQs test semantic memory while short answers test episodic memory
Recall only needs matching to a stored fact; recognition needs retrieval with few cues
Recognition only needs matching to a stored fact; recall needs retrieval with few cues
The options trigger false positives, so his MCQ scores are mostly luck
why: Recognition (MCQ) matches presented information to what is stored, while recall (short answer) has very few external cues, so retrieval failure is more likely. The definitions are swapped in the most tempting distractor.

q: Danial knows that Malaysia's independence day is 31 August 1957. He also remembers watching the Merdeka fireworks with his cousins last year. How should these two memories be classified?
opts: Semantic, then nondeclarative
Episodic, then semantic — both declarative
Semantic, then episodic — both declarative
Episodic, then episodic — both personal
why: General factual knowledge (the date) is semantic. A personal event only he experienced (fireworks with cousins) is episodic. Both are conscious, so both are declarative. The date is a shared fact, not a personal event, so 'episodic first' is wrong.

q: In Sperling's study, a grid of letters flashed briefly, then a tone signalled which row to report. Participants could report almost any cued row, but the longer the tone was delayed, the fewer letters they reported. What does this show?
opts: Iconic memory briefly holds the whole display, then fades very fast
An attention filter fully blocks the rows that were not cued
Echoic memory of the tone lasts longer than iconic memory
STM holds about 7 ± 2 letters regardless of the delay
why: Because any row could be reported when cued, the whole grid must have been in iconic memory. The quick drop with delay shows it lasts only about a quarter of a second. The 7 ± 2 limit describes STM, not this brief visual store.

q: After watching a video of a car accident, participants were asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other. A week later, many of them said they had seen broken glass, though there was none. Which conclusion does this support most directly?
opts: Unused memory traces decay over a week
The details were never encoded, so they were forgotten
Misleading information after an event can alter the memory of it
People falsely believe they could have predicted the outcome
why: The leading word 'smashed' was added after the event and changed what people later remembered — the misinformation effect, showing memory is reconstructed. Encoding failure would make them forget a detail, not add one that never existed.

q: After surgery that removed both hippocampi, a patient practised a mirror-drawing task each day and got steadily better, yet every day insisted he had never seen the task before. What does this pattern show?
opts: The cerebellum was removed, so he cannot form new skills
His short-term memory was destroyed by the surgery
The surgery caused retrograde amnesia for all old skills
New declarative memories need the hippocampus; skill memory does not
why: Like Patient H.M., he can form new nondeclarative (procedural) memories but not new declarative ones, showing the hippocampus is needed to consolidate new facts and events. Skill learning still improved, so the cerebellum/motor system clearly still worked.

q: After a motorbike accident, Danial cannot remember anything from the two weeks before the crash. However, he easily remembers the nurses, visitors and conversations he has had since waking up in hospital. What is he experiencing?
opts: Early-stage Alzheimer's disease
Retrograde amnesia
Anterograde amnesia
Infantile amnesia
why: Loss of memory going backwards from the injury is retrograde amnesia. Anterograde amnesia would mean he could NOT form new memories after the accident, but he forms them easily.

q: In a lab, a patient hears a tone that is always followed by a loud, startling horn. Later she can clearly state 'the tone comes before the horn', but her body shows no fear reaction at all when the tone plays. Damage to which structure best explains this?
opts: Hippocampus
Prefrontal cortex
Amygdala
Cerebellum
why: She can still form a new declarative fact (so the hippocampus works) but not a new emotional memory, which depends on the amygdala. Hippocampal damage would produce the opposite pattern — fear without conscious memory of the pairing.

q: Three of these are examples of declarative (explicit) memory. Which one is NOT?
opts: Remembering that your tutorial was moved to Room 3
Recalling the moment you opened your HELP offer letter
Knowing that the hippocampus helps form new memories
Feeling uneasy at the smell of clinic antiseptic without knowing why
why: An unexplained emotional reaction is a conditioned emotional association — nondeclarative memory that shows in behaviour without conscious awareness. The other three are consciously known facts or personal events, so they are declarative.

q: Every time Aina's mother uses the blender, she feeds the cat right afterwards. After a few weeks, the cat runs to the kitchen and drools as soon as it hears the blender. Which pair correctly labels the blender sound and the drooling to that sound?
opts: Conditioned stimulus; conditioned response
Neutral stimulus; unconditioned response
Unconditioned stimulus; unconditioned response
Conditioned stimulus; unconditioned response
why: The blender started as neutral but became a CS after pairing with food, and drooling to the blender is learned, so it is a CR. Drooling to food itself would be the UCR — drooling to the sound is not unlearned.

q: A Year 3 teacher gives pupils a sticker for each finished worksheet. On Friday, ten stickers can be traded for a canteen voucher. Which description fits this programme best?
opts: Shaping through successive approximations
Primary reinforcement of a biological need
Negative reinforcement of finishing work
A token economy using secondary reinforcers
why: Stickers gain value because they can be exchanged for something else, so they are secondary reinforcers in a token economy. Shaping would involve rewarding small steps towards a new complex behaviour, not rewarding each finished worksheet.

q: Encik Lim ate satay once and was violently sick that night because of a stomach virus. Now just the smell of satay makes him nauseous, even though he knows the satay wasn't the cause. What best explains this?
opts: Higher-order conditioning from the satay stall
Stimulus generalisation from earlier illnesses
Vicarious conditioning from watching others
Conditioned taste aversion after a single pairing
why: A taste followed once by nausea produces a lasting aversion — conditioned taste aversion, reflecting biological preparedness. Higher-order conditioning would need an already strong CS paired with a new neutral stimulus, which didn't happen here.

q: Mei Ling plays a mobile gacha game in which a rare character drops after an unpredictable number of paid pulls. Which pattern of playing is most likely?
opts: A pause after each drop, then a burst of pulls
A fast, steady rate with no pauses, hard to extinguish
Little play early on, then rapid pulls near a set time
A slow, steady rate because rewards depend on time
why: This is a variable ratio schedule: the number of responses needed changes each time, so there is no pause and the response rate is fast, like slot machines. A pause after each reward is the fixed ratio (stair-step) pattern.

q: Pavlov's dog salivates to a bell. The bell is then rung many times without food until salivation stops. The dog rests overnight, and the next morning the bell is rung again. What is most likely?
opts: No salivation, because extinction erased the learning
Salivation briefly reappears, usually weaker than before
Salivation returns at full strength and stays there
The dog salivates to every sound in the laboratory
why: This is spontaneous recovery: an extinguished response reappears after a rest, showing learning is a relatively permanent change that extinction does not erase. Responding to every sound would be generalisation, which isn't triggered by a rest period.

q: A PSY111 class has a quiz every Friday at 9 am, and it is the only time marks can be earned. What study pattern would you predict for most students across the week?
opts: Constant high-rate study all week with no pauses
Little study right after the quiz, rising steadily towards Friday
Study only after a set number of chapters are read
Random bursts of study unrelated to the quiz day
why: Reinforcement is only possible after a set amount of time, so this is a fixed interval schedule, which produces a pause after reinforcement and a scalloped rise as the time approaches. Constant high-rate responding is typical of variable schedules.

q: A rat is classically conditioned to fear a 1000 Hz tone paired with shock. It is then tested with a 1100 Hz tone and a 3000 Hz tone, neither paired with shock. What is the most likely result?
opts: More fear to 1100 Hz than to 3000 Hz
No fear to either, because they were never paired
More fear to 3000 Hz than to 1100 Hz
Equal fear to both new tones
