why: Stimulus generalisation, as in Hovland's study: the closer a stimulus is to the original CS, the stronger the response. Zero fear would reflect complete discrimination, which only develops after the similar tones are repeatedly shown NOT to predict shock.

q: Danial starts the car without his seat belt, and an annoying beeping alarm starts. He buckles up and the alarm stops. Soon he always buckles up first. Why is this negative reinforcement rather than punishment?
opts: An unpleasant stimulus is added, and not buckling decreases
A pleasant stimulus is removed, and buckling up decreases
An unpleasant stimulus is removed, and buckling up increases
The alarm is a primary reinforcer that follows buckling up
why: Reinforcement always increases a behaviour; 'negative' means something unpleasant is removed. The behaviour that increases (buckling up) is followed by the alarm stopping. Punishment would make a behaviour less likely, and the focus here is the behaviour that grows.

q: Puan Siti takes away her son's phone for a week after he comes home two hours late. Which label is correct, and why?
opts: Positive punishment — an unpleasant experience is added after the behaviour
Extinction — the reinforcement for coming home late has stopped
Negative punishment — a pleasant item is removed to reduce the behaviour
Negative reinforcement — something is removed to change the behaviour
why: Removing something pleasurable to make coming home late less likely is negative punishment. Negative reinforcement is the tempting trap: something is removed, but reinforcement always INCREASES a behaviour, and here she wants it to decrease.

q: A baby starts crying whenever a nurse in a white coat comes near (after several injections). A child tidies her room every Saturday to get pocket money. Which classification is correct?
opts: Both classical, because both involve a learned association
Baby: operant (crying is rewarded); child: classical (money is a UCS)
Baby: classical (elicited, involuntary); child: operant (emitted, voluntary)
Both operant, because both behaviours have consequences
why: The baby's crying is an involuntary response elicited by a stimulus (white coat) that came before it — classical. The child's voluntary tidying is controlled by the consequence (money) — operant. Crying isn't being kept going by a reward here, so the baby isn't operant.

q: Whenever Arif hits his sister, his mother sends him to sit alone in a quiet corner for five minutes, away from everyone's attention. Why is this time-out rather than simple extinction?
opts: It just stops rewarding the hitting, so the behaviour fades
It reinforces him for sitting quietly in the corner
It adds an unpleasant consequence after the hitting
It removes access to attention as a consequence, a mild punishment by removal
why: Time-out takes the child away from attention and other sources of reinforcement after the behaviour — negative punishment. Extinction would mean simply ignoring the hitting and letting it continue unreinforced, without removing him from anything.

q: Rescorla gave two groups of rats a long tone and a shock. In one group the shock came after the tone started; in the other, after the tone stopped. The first group feared the tone starting; the second feared the tone ending. What does this support?
opts: The tone became a second CS via higher-order conditioning
Rats are biologically prepared to fear sounds
Pairing in time alone is enough for conditioning
The CS works by giving information that the UCS is coming
why: Both groups had the tone and shock close in time, yet they learned different things depending on what predicted the shock. This supports the cognitive view that conditioning depends on expectancy. If timing alone mattered, both groups should have learned the same thing.

q: After Watson paired a white rat with a frightening loud noise, Little Albert feared the rat — and also a rabbit, a dog and a sealskin coat that had never been paired with the noise. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: The fear was instinctive drift back to an inborn pattern
A conditioned emotional response can generalise to similar stimuli
Albert learned the fear vicariously by watching Watson
Albert had learned to discriminate the rat from other furry objects
why: The fear was classically conditioned (a CER) and spread to stimuli similar to the rat — stimulus generalisation. Discrimination would be the opposite: responding ONLY to the rat and not to the similar objects.

q: Three of these are examples of positive reinforcement. Which one is NOT?
opts: Receiving a bonus for submitting a report early
Getting merit points for helping at a school event
Taking Panadol so that a pounding headache goes away
Being praised by a lecturer for a good answer
why: Taking Panadol is strengthened by REMOVING something unpleasant (the headache), so it is negative reinforcement. The other three add a pleasant stimulus after the behaviour.

q: Three of these are examples of classical conditioning. Which one is NOT?
opts: Mei Ling's heart races when she sees the lecturer's red pen
Mei Ling flinches at the sound of a dentist's drill
Mei Ling studies harder after her lecturer praises her essay
Mei Ling feels hungry at the sound of a wok at the kopitiam
why: Studying harder because of praise is a voluntary behaviour controlled by its consequence — operant conditioning. The other three are involuntary emotional or physical reactions triggered by a stimulus that was paired with something else.

q: Three of these show problems with severe punishment. Which one does NOT?
opts: A child who is often caned starts hitting younger children
A child stops at once because the punishment is immediate and consistent
A child lies about a broken vase to avoid being caned
A child avoids his father rather than stopping the misbehaviour
why: Immediate, consistent punishment is how punishment is made effective, not a problem with it. Lying, avoiding the punisher and modelling aggression are listed problems with severe punishment.

q: During orientation week, Danial wanders around the HELP campus with no particular aim. A month later, a friend says there is free food in a hall he 'explored' once, and he immediately takes the shortest route there. Which kind of learning does this show?
opts: Insight learning
Observational learning
Latent learning
Learned helplessness
why: He learned the campus layout without any reward, and the learning only showed when it became useful (free food) — like Tolman's rats. Insight would be a sudden solution to a problem, but he didn't have to solve anything; he already knew the way.

q: Aina failed Add Maths repeatedly in secondary school despite trying hard. In university, she is placed in a much easier statistics course, but she skips the tutorials and says, 'No point, I'm just bad at maths.' What best explains her behaviour?
opts: Negative reinforcement
The learning/performance distinction
Latent learning
Learned helplessness
why: A history of repeated failure has taught her that effort makes no difference, so she fails to act even when success is now possible — learned helplessness. The learning/performance distinction is about learning a behaviour without performing it, not giving up because of past failure.

q: Mei Ling spent an hour stuck on a logic puzzle and finally gave up. While walking to the LRT, she suddenly sees how the pieces relate to each other and knows the whole answer at once. What is this?
opts: Trial-and-error learning
Observational learning
Insight
Latent learning
why: A sudden perception of the relationships among parts of a problem, giving a quick solution, is insight — the 'aha' moment Köhler described. Trial and error is the opposite: trying solutions one after another until one happens to work.

q: In a Bobo doll study, children saw a model punished for hitting the doll, and they did not copy the aggression. The experimenter then offers each child a sticker for every aggressive action they can show. What is most likely?
opts: They only copy the model's non-aggressive play
They become helpless and refuse to do anything
They now reproduce the aggressive acts accurately
They still cannot show any aggressive acts
why: This is the learning/performance distinction: the children had learned the aggressive acts, but did not perform them until there was a reward. If they truly couldn't show any aggression, it would mean nothing had been learned — which Bandura's results contradict.

q: In Seligman's study, Group A dogs were held in a harness and received shocks they could not escape. They are then placed in a two-sided box where jumping a low hurdle avoids the shock. What will they most likely do?
opts: Quickly jump the hurdle to the safe side
Jump the hurdle only after watching another dog
Escape at once through sudden insight
Stay on the shock side and not try to escape
why: Dogs that had learned escape was impossible stayed where the shock was — learned helplessness. Quick jumping is what the control group (no inescapable shock) did.

q: Köhler's chimpanzee, after failing to reach a banana, sat still for a while and then stacked boxes and climbed up to get it. Why is this insight rather than latent learning?
opts: The solution came suddenly from seeing how the parts of the problem related
The behaviour was slowly shaped through rewarded steps
Learning stayed hidden until a reward made it worth showing
The chimp copied a model it had seen stacking boxes
why: Insight is the sudden perception of relationships among the parts of a problem. Latent learning means the knowledge already existed but was hidden until a reward made it useful — the chimp hadn't previously learned to stack boxes for food.

q: In Tolman and Honzik's study, Group 2 rats were first rewarded on Day 11, and on Day 12 their errors dropped to the level of the always-rewarded group. Why is this evidence of latent learning, not just fast learning once food appeared?
opts: The drop was too quick to start from scratch; they had learned in Days 1–10
The rats suddenly saw how the maze fitted together
They watched Group 1 run the maze and copied the route
Food is a primary reinforcer, so it makes learning extremely fast
why: Learning a maze from zero takes many rewarded trials (Group 1 took days), so an instant drop means the map was already learned without reward. The 'primary reinforcer' idea can't explain matching days of practice in a single trial.

q: Tolman's rats learned a maze without being rewarded and only showed it when food was introduced. Which view does this finding most clearly CHALLENGE?
opts: Cognition must be included to explain learning
Learning involves mental events like a map of the maze
Learning requires reinforcement and is just observable behaviour
Learning can stay hidden until it becomes useful
why: Early behaviourism held that learning was observable behaviour shaped by reinforcement; rats learning with no reward and no visible change challenge that. The other options are what the study SUPPORTS — the cognitive view.

q: In Bandura's original Bobo doll study, children who watched an adult kick and hit the doll later did the same, using the same actions, even though they had never been rewarded for it. What does this most directly support?
opts: Aggression is a conditioned emotional response to the doll
New behaviour can be learned by watching a model
Aggression is learned only through direct reinforcement
Children are biologically prepared to be aggressive
why: The children copied specific new actions they had only observed, with no reinforcement of their own — observational learning. Direct reinforcement can't explain it, because the children were never rewarded for hitting.

q: Dogs that had been given inescapable shocks did not try to escape later, while dogs without that history escaped easily. Which conclusion follows most directly?
opts: Past experiences of no control can stop later attempts to act
Shock is a stronger reinforcer for some dogs than for others
Dogs learn to escape best by watching other dogs
The tone became a CS that made dogs more active
why: Seligman concluded that a history of failing to escape led the dogs to stop trying even when escape was possible — learned helplessness. Nothing in the study involved watching other dogs, so observational learning isn't the conclusion.

q: Arif watches a YouTube chef make roti canai. Three of these would stop him from reproducing it through observational learning. Which one would NOT?
opts: He forgot the order of the steps by the next day
He was scrolling his phone while the dough was flipped
He expects his family to praise him if he makes it
His hands can't yet stretch the dough thin enough
why: Expecting praise means motivation is present, which helps performance. The others are failures of attention, memory/retention and motoric reproduction — three of Bandura's four elements.

q: Three of these are examples of cognitive learning (latent, insight or observational). Which one is NOT?
opts: A child says 'please' more often after getting a sweet each time
A rat learns a maze while exploring with no reward
A teenager learns a TikTok dance by watching it
A chimp suddenly stacks boxes to reach a banana
why: Saying 'please' more because it is followed by sweets is operant conditioning: behaviour shaped directly by its consequence. The other three are insight, observational and latent learning, which emphasise mental events.

q: At a picnic, there's no knife to cut the birthday cake. Danial says they can't cut it, but his friend slices it neatly with the edge of a plastic card. Which barrier was stopping Danial?
opts: Mental set
Availability heuristic
Confirmation bias
Functional fixedness
why: Danial thought of the card only in terms of its usual function (payment), not as a cutting tool — functional fixedness. Mental set is about sticking with problem-solving methods that worked before, not an object's typical use.

q: After seeing news of a plane crash, Puan Siti cancels her flight to Penang and drives five hours instead, even though road travel causes far more deaths per trip. Which process best explains her choice?
opts: Availability heuristic
Functional fixedness
Confirmation bias
Representativeness heuristic
why: She judged flying as more dangerous because a vivid example came to mind easily — the availability heuristic. Representativeness is about judging whether something belongs to a category because it resembles it, not about how easily examples come to mind.

q: Aina walks into a mamak she's never been to. Without thinking, she sits down, calls the waiter, orders teh tarik, eats, then goes to the counter to pay. Which concept guides her behaviour?
opts: An algorithm
A prototype
A formal concept
A script
why: A script is a type of schema for a familiar sequence of activities, like eating at a mamak. A prototype is the best example of a category (e.g. an apple for 'fruit'), not a sequence of actions.

q: Participants memorise a map of an island with a hut, a nearby rock and a distant tree. They are asked to mentally travel from the hut to each landmark. What result would Kosslyn et al. predict?
opts: Both trips take the same time, as images have no distance
Reaching the tree takes longer than reaching the rock
Times are random because imagery is not spatial
Reaching the rock takes longer as it's smaller
why: Kosslyn found that the greater the distance on the memorised map, the longer the mental trip — mental images keep spatial properties like real pictures. Equal times would only happen if images had no spatial layout.

q: Puan Siti's son is about 18 months old and is developing typically. Which utterance is he most likely to produce?
opts: "Daddy is going to work in the car."
Soft vowel sounds like "ooo" and "aah"
"Ba-ba-ba-da-da."
"Daddy go car."
why: At around 1.5 years, children typically use telegraphic speech: short strings of key words with grammar words left out. Babbling (consonant-vowel sounds) is typical at about 6 months, and full sentences come in the preschool years.

q: In a maths tutorial, Danial keeps using a long method that worked on the last ten questions, missing an obvious shortcut on the new question. Why is this mental set rather than functional fixedness?
opts: He's judging the question by how easily similar ones come to mind
He's relying on an algorithm, which always finds the answer
He's only using evidence that agrees with what he already believes
He's sticking to a past strategy, not seeing an object only by its usual use
why: Mental set means persisting with problem-solving patterns that worked before. Functional fixedness is specifically about thinking of OBJECTS only in their typical function, and no object is involved here.

q: Encik Lim sees a quiet man with glasses reading a thick book in the library and is sure he must be a lecturer, not a businessman, even though there are far more businessmen in KL. Which heuristic is this, and why?
opts: Availability — lecturers come to mind more easily in a library
Representativeness — he matches Encik Lim's image of a lecturer
Availability — he has recently met many lecturers
Representativeness — lecturers are far more common in KL
why: He is assuming the man belongs to a category because he shares its typical characteristics — representativeness. Availability would rely on how easily examples come to mind, but the judgement here comes from resemblance.

q: The Dani people of New Guinea have only two colour words, yet they perceive and remember colours in much the same way English speakers do. Which view does this finding support?
opts: Vygotsky's language-first view
Linguistic relativity
Cognitive universalism
The availability heuristic
why: If language controlled thought (linguistic relativity), having two colour words should change colour perception — it didn't. Universal concepts seem to shape perception regardless of vocabulary, supporting cognitive universalism.

q: In Gelman and Markman's (1986) study, children were told a new bird was a 'blackbird'. They more often said it fed its babies mashed-up food, like another blackbird, even though it looked more like a different bird. What does this suggest?
opts: A label can shape how children reason about a category
Language has no effect on how children think
Children rely only on appearance to make inferences
Concepts always develop before language, as Piaget said
why: The shared name shaped the children's inference more than appearance did, supporting a version of linguistic relativity for higher-level concepts. Relying only on appearance is exactly what the children did NOT do.

q: A large meta-analysis (Gunnerud et al., 2020) pooled many studies comparing bilingual and monolingual children on executive function. Which conclusion is most consistent with its findings?
opts: Bilingualism prevents cognitive decline in all adults
The overall bilingual advantage is negligible
Bilingualism greatly improves all executive functions
Bilingualism clearly harms executive function
why: The meta-analysis found that the overall advantages were negligible, despite the popular claims about better executive function. It did not show harm either — just no meaningful overall difference.

q: Three of these are examples of divergent thinking. Which one is NOT?
opts: Brainstorming names for the Psychology Student Union
Mind-mapping ideas for a PSY111 exhibition booth
Listing 30 unusual uses for an old brick
Using the quadratic formula to find the one correct answer
why: Using a formula and logic to reach a single right answer is convergent thinking. The others start from one point and produce many different ideas, which is divergent thinking.

q: Three of these words contain exactly two morphemes. Which one does NOT?
opts: elephant
unkind
books
playing
why: 'Elephant' is a single unit of meaning — its parts don't carry meaning on their own. 'Play + ing', 'book + s' and 'un + kind' each combine two morphemes, like the lecture example 'playing'.
